text:
The normal. It's what you get when many small, independent effects add up. Take the flippers of a hundred and fifty-one Adelie penguins. Each is the sum of countless small nudges... and together they come out close to a bell. Two numbers set it. The mean puts the center, at a hundred and ninety millimeters. The standard deviation sets the spread, here six and a half. And with those two numbers, every normal shares one fact.

About sixty-eight percent of it lies within one standard deviation of the mean. Ninety-five percent lies within two. And ninety-nine point seven within three. So if test scores average a hundred, with a spread of fifteen, ninety-five percent land between seventy and a hundred and thirty. And a hundred and forty-five, three out, is genuinely rare. That ruler works on any normal, once a value is measured in standard deviations.

That's its z-score. A score of a hundred and thirty sits thirty points above the mean, two standard deviations. Its z is two. But a z of two isn't a two percent chance. It's a position. Look up the area to its left, and ninety-seven point seven percent of scores fall below it. That only works when the data really is normal, though.

Here are five thousand incomes, with a long tail of high earners. The mean is forty-three thousand, but the median is under thirty-six thousand. Force a normal onto them anyway, with the same mean and spread... and it puts six percent of people below zero, earning less than nothing. So don't assume normal. It's something you check, with a plot. And checking a model starts with fitting one.
